title_en: Synodal Letter to the Bishops of Africa
author: Athanasius of Alexandria
occasion: Athanasius and the bishops of Egypt and Libya write to the African bishops to warn them against those who appeal to the Council of Ariminum instead of Nicaea, and to confirm the sufficiency of the Nicene faith.
argument: The Nicene Council is the one ecumenical and sufficient confession of the faith, received from Christ, the apostles, and the Fathers. Later councils, especially Ariminum, were contrived by Arians out of rivalry and violence, and their leaders were deposed. The Nicene terms 'from the substance' and 'consubstantial' were chosen to exclude Arian evasions and express what Scripture teaches about the Son. Those who reject Nicaea are heirs of Arius and should be rejected.

outline.move: The letter opens by affirming the sufficiency of Nicaea and the worldwide agreement with it, while warning against those who prefer the Council of Ariminum.
Athanasius contrasts Nicaea's legitimate occasion with the many later councils made from rivalry and violence, and recounts the deposition of Arian leaders at Ariminum.

He argues that the Nicene Fathers spoke from Scripture in confessing the Son's substance and hypostasis, while the Arians, by rejecting these terms and saying God has no substance or hypostasis, effectively say with the fool 'There is no God'—not that they deny God's existence outright, but their position leads to that conclusion.
He explains how the Nicene phrase 'from the substance of God' was chosen to counter Arian misuse of 'from God' and other scriptural expressions.
He shows that 'consubstantial' was not invented by the bishops but received from earlier Fathers, and challenges opponents to explain how the Son is one with the Father.
He argues that the Son's divine attributes cannot come from virtue or participation but belong to him by nature, proving he is consubstantial with the Father.

He concludes that 'consubstantial' is the proper mark of the Son's relation to the Father, urges the Africans to hold to Nicaea alone and reject later rival councils, and reports that the Egyptian and Libyan bishops have written to Damasus of Rome about Auxentius of Milan, noting his Arian communion and crimes with Gregory, and expressing wonder that he has not yet been deposed; he thanks Damasus and the Roman synod for expelling Ursacius, Valens, and their fellows.
He closes by confessing the full Nicene faith in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and praying that the Africans keep the tradition delivered to them.

cast.name: Athanasius
cast.who: Bishop of Alexandria and principal author of the letter.

cast.name: Damasus
cast.who: Bishop of Rome, whose synodal letter is praised.

cast.name: Auxentius
cast.who: Arian bishop who intruded into the church of Milan.

cast.name: Constantius
cast.who: Emperor who ordered the Council of Ariminum and supported the Arians.

cast.name: Eusebius
cast.who: Eusebius of Caesarea, who was formerly aligned with the Arian heresy but signed at Nicaea and later wrote to his own people affirming that ancient bishops and writers had used the term 'consubstantial'.

cast.name: Gregory
cast.who: Associate of Auxentius in impiety and wrongdoing.

voices.speaker: Arian opponents (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by phrases such as 'they say' or 'they will say' and by direct quotation of their slogans.

voices.speaker: Scripture (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'saying', 'as it is written', or direct quotation from biblical books.

voices.speaker: The Nicene Fathers (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'they wrote', 'they confessed', or direct quotation of the creed and anathemas. Note that section 4 quotes their reasoning process and deliberation rather than a formal quotation; the actual creed formula appears in sections 3, 5, 7, 8.

key_terms.sense: The Son is of the same substance or being as the Father, not merely similar or created.
The underlying being or substance of God, which the Son shares with the Father.
The actual existence or subsistence of God, equated here with substance.
A created thing; the Arians wrongly call the Son a creature.
Something made; used by Arians to deny the Son's uncreated divinity.
The Arian slogan that the Son came into being from nothing, not from God's being.
The Arian slogan that there was a time when the Son did not exist.
candidates: there was when he was not

key_terms.sense: Things that have come into being, created and changeable, unlike the uncreated Son.
Radiance or reflection, used of the Son's relation to the Father's glory.
Exact imprint or representation, used of the Son as the perfect expression of the Father's being.
The universal council, specifically Nicaea, whose authority is binding on the whole church.
The heresy of Arius that denies the Son's true divinity and consubstantiality with the Father.
The sound or healthy faith, the orthodox teaching handed down from the apostles and Fathers.
The universal church, whose faith is expressed at Nicaea and whose unity Athanasius seeks to preserve.

scripture: The author uses Septuagint book names and Psalm numbering. Citations should be given in modern form, e.g. LXX Psalm numbering corresponds to the traditional Greek numbering; where a modern English Bible differs, note the LXX numbering. New Testament citations follow standard book names.
uncertain: The exact date of composition is approximate.
The precise identity of Gregory, the associate of Auxentius, is not fully certain.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Eudoxius ... Arian leader condemned at Ariminum.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Οὐρσάκιος καὶ Οὐάλης, Εὐδόξιος καὶ Αὐξέντιος, ἐκεῖ δὲ ἦν σὺν αὐτοῖς καὶ Δημόφιλος, καθῃρέθησαν, θελήσαντες ἕτερα παρὰ τὰ ἐν Νικαίᾳ γράφειν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Eudoxius was present at Ariminum and deposed there for trying to write something different from Nicaea, but the source does not explicitly call him an 'Arian leader'—he is grouped with others who were deposed.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Constantius ... Emperor who ordered the Council of Ariminum and supported the Arians.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ταῦτα καὶ Κωνσταντίῳ δεδηλώκασι, τῷ καὶ τὴν σύνοδον κελεύσαντι γενέσθαι. Ἀλλ' οἱ ἐν τῇ Ἀριμήνῳ καθαιρεθέντες, ἀπελθόντες πρὸς Κωνστάντιον, πεποιήκασιν ὑβρισθῆναι μὲν, ἀπειλὰς δὲ γενέσθαι
_unresolved_facts.fix: Constantius ordered the council to be held, but the source emphasizes that the deposed bishops went to Constantius and caused threats and violence against the orthodox bishops; the source does not say Constantius 'supported the Arians' directly, though this is implied by his actions after the deposed bishops appealed to him.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Eusebius ... Eusebius of Caesarea, who was formerly aligned with the Arian heresy but signed at Nicaea and later wrote to his own people affirming that ancient bishops and writers had used the term 'consubstantial'.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Εὐσέβιος ὁ γενόμενος ἐπίσκοπος τῆς Καισαρείας, πρότερον μὲν συντρέχων τῇ Ἀρειανῇ αἱρέσει, ὕστερον δὲ ὑπογράψας ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ ἐν Νικαίᾳ συνόδῳ, ἔγραψε τοῖς ἰδίοις διαβεβαιούμενος, ὅτι καὶ τῶν παλαιῶν τινας λογίους καὶ ἐπιφανεῖς ἐπισκόπους καὶ συγγραφέας, ἔγνωμεν ἐπὶ τῆς τοῦ Πατρὸς καὶ Υἱοῦ θεότητος τῷ τοῦ ὁμοουσίου χρησαμένους ὀνόματι
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source says Eusebius wrote to his own people (τοῖς ἰδίοις) affirming that they knew (ἔγνωμεν) that some ancient learned and notable bishops and writers had used the term 'consubstantial'—not that he himself affirmed this, but that he reported what 'we knew' (presumably the Nicene bishops or himself included).

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Συνθώμεθα· καὶ γὰρ καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐσμεν· εἷς γὰρ Θεός, ἐξ οὗ τὰ πάντα· καὶ, Τὰ ἀρχαῖα παρῆλθεν, ἰδοὺ γέγονε τὰ πάντα καινά. Τὰ δὲ πάντα ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ ... καὶ ταῦτα φθάνει καὶ εἰς ἡμᾶς· καὶ γὰρ καὶ ἡμεῖς καὶ εἰκὼν καὶ δόξα Θεοῦ λεγόμεθα ... Ἀεὶ γὰρ ἡμεῖς οἱ ζῶντες. Καὶ δυνάμεις πολλαί εἰσι ... οὐ λυπεῖ ἡμᾶς· γενόμενος γὰρ, ἀληθινός ἐστιν
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Arian opponents' voice appears in section 4, not section 5. Section 5 contains Athanasius's argument against the Arians, not their direct quotations. The sections should be ['4'] for Arian opponents.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: section 4 contains reasoning about why the bishops wrote 'from the substance' and 'consubstantial'—this is Athanasius narrating their deliberation, not quoting their formal voice
_unresolved_facts.fix: Section 4 does not contain formal quotations of the Nicene Fathers' voice; it contains Athanasius's narrative explanation of their reasoning process. The actual creed formula and anathemas appear in sections 3, 5, 7, 8. Section 4 should be removed or noted as containing narrative about rather than quotation of the Fathers.

_unresolved_facts.claim: section 3: 'not that they deny God's existence outright, but their position leads to that conclusion'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: λέγοντες καὶ αὐτοὶ, ὡς ἄφρων ἐν καρδίᾳ, Οὐκ ἔστι Θεός
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source says they speak 'as the fool in his heart, There is no God'—this is a direct scriptural quotation (Psalm 13:1/52:1) applied to them. The source does not qualify this with 'not that they deny God's existence outright'; Athanasius is saying their position is equivalent to saying 'there is no God' in the sense of denying the true God, not making a nuanced distinction about outright denial versus conclusion.

_unresolved_facts.claim: section 7: 'reports that the Egyptian and Libyan bishops have written to Damasus of Rome about Auxentius of Milan'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐγράψαμεν καὶ τῷ ἀγαπητῷ ἡμῶν Δαμάσῳ τῷ ἐπισκόπῳ τῆς μεγάλης Ῥώμης περὶ τοῦ Αὐξεντίου
_unresolved_facts.fix: Athanasius says 'we wrote' (ἐγράψαμεν), not 'the Egyptian and Libyan bishops have written' as a separate group. The letter is from Athanasius and the 90 bishops together, and he includes this as part of their own action, not as a separate report about others' actions.
